claims.text: The equiatomic Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni alloy can be investigated in an FCC state.
Quaternary and ternary subsets can all be prepared as single-phase FCC materials with comparable grain sizes.
Increasing the number of constituents increases local lattice distortion.
Constituent count controls the extent or complexity of short-range chemical order.
Local lattice distortion and short-range order alter dislocation core structures.
The quinary alloy has greater local lattice distortion than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Greater lattice distortion creates a rugged dislocation-energy landscape.
Greater lattice distortion and more complex short-range order spread dislocation cores and restrict cross-slip.
Restricted cross-slip in the quinary alloy favors uniform slip with lower work hardening.
Reducing the constituent count decreases local lattice distortion.
Reduced lattice distortion in quaternary and ternary alloys facilitates twinning and cross-slip.
Enhanced twinning and cross-slip increase strain hardening and ductility in the lower-constituent alloys.
The quinary alloy will have higher yield strength than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary alloy will have lower strain hardening and ductility than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
The quinary alloy will exhibit more restricted dislocation mobility and fewer deformation twins than the lower-constituent subsets.
The controlled investigation should compare alloys with matched processing history, grain size, phase purity, and microstructural homogeneity.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply from room temperature to approximately 700 °C at low to moderate strain rates.
Secondary phases, extreme strain rates, and environmental effects are outside the proposed mechanism's scope.

A lack of correlation between mechanical-property differences and lattice distortion, short-range order, or dislocation-core structure, together with no predicted shift in deformation mode, would falsify the hypothesis.
